issues.legal_issue: Failure to pursue an available intermediate appeal does not create an absolute bar to special leave or require its automatic revocation.
material_facts: The challenged decision was made by a single judge in a second appeal.
The appellants did not seek leave to pursue an appeal to a division bench under the available Letters Patent procedure before seeking special leave.
The court found the second-appellate judgment’s defect sufficiently serious to warrant setting aside the decree and remitting the matter.
issues.conclusion: The failure to pursue the Letters Patent remedy did not, by itself, require dismissal of the appeal or revocation of special leave; whether to exercise jurisdiction under Article 136 depended on the facts of the case.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court has wide discretion over whether to exercise its jurisdiction and on what terms. A party would normally be expected to pursue an available Letters Patent appeal before seeking special leave from a second-appellate decision, but there is no inflexible rule barring special leave or requiring its revocation for failure to do so. Article 133(3) reflects the general position against appeals to the Supreme Court from a judgment of one High Court judge. Raruha Singh v. Achal Singh was considered, but its statement about already-granted leave was not treated as laying down an absolute rule.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_second_appella: A party seeks special leave to appeal from a decision made in a second appeal.
predicates.intermediate_appellate_remedy_not_pursue: The party did not pursue an available appeal to an intermediate appellate bench before seeking special leave.

issues.definition: When a party seeks special leave from a second-appellate decision without pursuing an available intermediate appeal, the court decides whether to exercise its jurisdiction on the case facts rather than applying an automatic bar or revocation.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent who contests special leave on the ground that an intermediate appeal was not pursued cannot raise that same objection again at the final hearing if the court rejected it when granting leave.
material_facts: The respondents objected at the final hearing that the appellants had not sought leave to appeal to a division bench under the Letters Patent.
The court explained that the record and circumstances at the time special leave was granted determine whether that objection may be raised at the final hearing.
issues.conclusion: The objection may not be raised again if it was argued and rejected on its merits when special leave was granted; if it was not decided at that stage, it may be raised at the final hearing.
issues.legal_principle: A point argued and decided against a respondent at the special-leave stage cannot be reopened at the final hearing. If the respondent did not appear, did not raise the point, or the court did not decide it before granting leave, there is no technical bar of res judicata and the point may be considered at the final hearing.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.respondent_objected_to_unpursued_interme: The respondent argued that the appellant had failed to pursue an available intermediate appeal.
predicates.objection_rejected_when_leave_granted: The court rejected that objection on its merits when granting special leave.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, a respondent who raised and lost an objection about an unpursued intermediate appeal when leave was granted cannot raise the same objection again at the final hearing.

issues.legal_issue: A decree in a second appeal that states a conclusion without giving substantive reasons does not satisfy the basic requirements of a judgment and must be set aside for lawful redetermination.
material_facts: A single judge heard a second appeal and stated only that, after considering the issues, a particular form of decree was appropriate.
The judge then set out the decree without explaining the reasoning supporting it.
The Supreme Court found that the approach resembled an unreasoned arbitral award and that the defect required the matter to be dealt with again in accordance with law.
issues.conclusion: The second-appellate decree was set aside and the matter was remitted to the High Court for disposal in accordance with law, without expressing an opinion on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: A judgment under the Code of Civil Procedure must meet its basic and legitimate requirements, including giving reasons for its conclusions. In a second appeal, the High Court must act within the limitations imposed by section 100 of the Code and follow the established procedure; it cannot substitute an unexplained decree for a judicial determination.

predicates.second_appeal_before_high_court: The proceeding is a second appeal before a High Court.
predicates.decree_disposed_without_substantive_reas: The judge states the result and frames a decree without explaining the reasons for the decision.

issues.definition: When a High Court disposes of a second appeal by decree without substantive reasons, the decree is set aside and the matter is returned for lawful disposal.
